newsitem.title: UK: British motorways and Heathrow hit by bomb threats.
newsitem.headline: British motorways and Heathrow hit by bomb threats.

text.p: Suspected IRA bomb threats on Tuesday paralysed large stretches of four major motorways into London just 48 hours before the British election.
Heathrow airport also received threatening phone calls, forcing a partial evacuation of a terminal used for flights to Europe, an airport spokesman said.

Thousands of commuters driving into the British capital were trapped in the traffic chaos but Prime Minister John Major vowed the government would never bow to pressure from Irish Republican Army guerrillas.

"I don't think the British people are going to be moved by this, they have made their judgement of the IRA. They cannot use the ballot box in Northern Ireland and bombs there and elsewhere. You can't cow the British people like this," Major told BBC radio.

Police said they received coded warnings that forced them to close parts of the M-1 motorway leading into London from northern England and the M-25 ring road around the capital which links up to the Channel ports as well as Heathrow and Gatwick airports.
"Britain's biggest by-pass could today become Britain's biggest traffic jam," warned a spokesman for the Royal Automobile Club motoring organisation.
Parts of the M-20 and the M-26 were also shut, bringing gridlock on roads to Dover and the south-east coast.
Police said that more than 50 miles (80 km) of motorway were affected by the alerts.
The IRA, fighting to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, has during the election campaign staged a string of bomb attacks and hoaxes on roads, railways and airports.

The guerrillas also forced the abandonment of the Grand National, the world's most famous steeplechase, with a telephoned threat that forced the evacuation of 70,000 racegoers from Aintree racecourse in northern England.
The IRA consider the tactic an ideal propaganda tool as it causes maximum disruption and minimal casualties.
The latest alerts that spelt misery for morning commuters in a now familiar pattern also provoked an angry response from Home Secretary Michael Howard.

"The one clear message we have to give the IRA is that the British people will never give in to pressure of this kind. What they are doing is utterly futile. It is a complete waste of time," he told GMTV television.
"It will not help them to achieve any of their objectives. We will never give in to that kind of pressure."
Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, is bidding to land three seats in the British parliament in Thursday's election.
The party, banned from Northern Ireland peace talks until the IRA calls a permanent ceasefire, hopes that a strong election result can put pressure on the new British government to back down.
